deep.reconstruction: Context: Euler is explaining why finding provably prime numbers beyond the existing tables is hard. Tables then reached about 100,000, with a recent one running to 101,000. Extending a table by the usual sieve, striking out every number divisible by a prime below its square root, would be immense labour. He predicts no one would push it past a million, so that exhibiting a prime above a million would seem impossible. He then announces his own method. With not very tedious computation it yields several numbers above 100,000, and even above 1,000,000, that he can assert with certainty are prime. He says it rests on number-theoretic properties that may be useful elsewhere. The method starts from numbers of the form a^2+1. For even a these contain many primes; for odd a the half (a^2+1)/2 does. He set out to find all divisors of numbers a^2+1. This does not require trial division by every prime up to about a. He had proved, after Fermat, whose proof is lost, that every divisor of a^2+1 is itself a sum of two squares. The next page draws the consequence: every odd prime divisor is of the form 4n+1. The procedure then inverts the problem. For each prime p = 4n+1, find all a with p | a^2+1; the solutions form two residue classes mod p, built from p = r^2+s^2. Strike out those a. The values of a^2+1 (or (a^2+1)/2) that are never struck out, below the square of the largest prime used, are prime. In modern terms this is a sieve over the values of the quadratic polynomial a^2+1. It uses the fact that the prime divisors of that polynomial are restricted to the primes that split in Z[i].
errors: Euler's rhetoric overstates the difficulty. Proving that one given number near 10^6 is prime by trial division needs at most 168 divisions, by the primes below 1000. That is tedious but hardly 'impossible'. The real difficulty he has in mind is producing a whole table, or sieving systematically. Euler himself later (1772) verified that 2^31-1 is prime, far above a million.
The 'radice a minores' bound is slightly loose: the trial-division bound for a^2+1 is sqrt(a^2+1), which differs negligibly from a. This is harmless.

ideas.what: Every divisor of a^2+1 is a sum of two squares; hence every odd prime divisor is of the form 4n+1.
ideas.modern_name: Fermat's two-squares theorem / splitting of primes in Z[i]; -1 is a quadratic residue mod p iff p ≡ 1 mod 4
ideas.where_published: E228 'De numeris qui sunt aggregata duorum quadratorum'; E241 'Demonstratio theorematis Fermatiani omnem numerum primum formae 4n+1 esse summam duorum quadratorum'

ideas.what: Sieving the values of a quadratic polynomial (a^2+1) by only the admissible primes, each removing two residue classes of a, in order to locate large primes.
ideas.modern_name: Polynomial sieve (precursor of sieving ideas used in Landau's n^2+1 problem and in the quadratic sieve)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E283) is known for this; widely discussed in the historical literature on prime tables
ideas.where_published: E283 itself, Novi Commentarii 9 (1764); discussed in Dickson's History vol. 1 and in Lemmermeyer's/Sandifer's accounts

ideas.what: Remark that a^2+1 for even a, and (a^2+1)/2 for odd a, contain many primes.
ideas.modern_name: Primes of the form n^2+1 (Landau's fourth problem; Hardy–Littlewood conjecture F)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known introduction of Euler's a^2+1 sieve for large primes, already documented in Dickson and in standard Euler histories. Nothing on the page is new or uncredited.
